title: Black Mulberry: Ancient Mulberries You Can Visit
meta_description: James I ordered mulberries planted across Britain in 1608 to start a silk industry, and got the species wrong. The trees outlived the plan.
intro: Britain's silk industry failed on a species error and left the trees behind. In 1608 James I ordered mulberries planted across the country to feed silkworms, but silkworms eat white mulberry and mostly refuse black, and black was what went into the ground. Charlton House got one of them and it is still fruiting four centuries later. Christ's College in Cambridge planted another in 1608 or 1609, the year after John Milton was born, and it is now reckoned at 417 years. Nothing here will look large. Mulberries do not build thick trunks, which is why Belgium's national champion measures 1.28 metres around and reads as unremarkable beside almost anything else in the same park. Breda's public library was designed around three of them rather than the other way round. Eight mapped, in five cities, and four of the eight are in London.
